b: Primary dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation without pelvic pathology, commonly after ovulatory cycles become established. Progesterone withdrawal increases endometrial prostaglandins, causing uterine hypercontractility, vasoconstriction a

Secondary dysmenorrhoea results from pathology such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID or obstructive Müllerian anomaly. Clues: new onset after years of painless periods, progressive pain, dyspareunia, infertility, abnormal bleedi

NSAIDs are first-line for primary dysmenorrhoea when safe; start at onset or shortly before predictable menstruation. Hormonal contraception/progestogens can suppress ovulation and reduce endometrial prostaglandins.
Investigate/treat secondary causes; persistent symptoms need review and imaging.

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with a history of dysmenorrhoea presents with cyclical lower abdominal pain that has worsened over the last 6 months. She also reports deep dyspareunia and dyschezia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: The combination of cyclical dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and dyschezia strongly suggests endometriosis, where endometrial-like tissue is found outside the uterus.
qs.s: Pelvic Pain in Gynaecology: Acute and Chronic Assessment,: MCQs

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman complains of cyclical dysmenorrhoea and a tender, bulky uterus on examination. Her periods are also heavy. What is the most likely gynaecological condition?
qs.e: Heavy painful periods (dysmenorrhoea) and a tender, bulky uterus are characteristic findings of adenomyosis, where endometrial tissue is found within the myometrium.
qs.s: Pelvic Pain in Gynaecology: Acute and Chronic Assessment,: MCQs

qs.q: A 30‑year‑old woman with chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia has a normal pelvic examination. Which imaging modality is best for mapping possible endometriosis?
qs.e: MRI provides detailed soft‑tissue contrast useful for delineating endometriotic lesions. Ultrasound is less sensitive for deep infiltrating disease, and CT or X‑ray are not appropriate.
qs.s: Pelvic Pain in Gynaecology: Acute and Chronic Assessment,: MCQs

qs.q: A 27‑year‑old woman presents with dysmenorrhoea, heavy bleeding and a uniformly enlarged, tender, boggy uterus on examination. Which diagnosis is most likely?
qs.e: The described uterine texture and symptom pattern fit adenomyosis rather than focal fibroids.
qs.s: Uterine Fibroids (Leiomyomas): Classification, Clinical Features,: MCQs

qs.q: A woman describes menstrual pain that starts before bleeding and is relieved by NSAIDs. Which type of dysmenorrhoea does this most likely represent?
qs.e: Pain that begins with the menstrual flow and responds to NSAIDs is typical of primary dysmenorrhoea due to prostaglandins. Secondary causes usually have additional features such as dyspareunia or irregular bleeding.

exam: What is the first‑line pharmacologic treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea and why? — NSAIDs; they inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, the main pain driver.
A 28‑year‑old woman with severe cramps and a 6‑cm ovarian cyst on ultrasound: what is your next step? — Refer for surgical evaluation; cyst may cause secondary dysmenorrhoea.

How would you differentiate dysmenorrhoea from acute appendicitis in a patient with right lower‑quadrant pain? — Timing with menses, response to NSAIDs, absence of fever/leukocytosis points to dysmenorrhoea.

Why might combined oral contraceptives be contraindicated in a woman with a history of deep‑vein thrombosis? — Estrogen increases clotting risk; alternatives like progestin‑only pills or IUS are safer.
In a low‑resource clinic without ultrasound, what clinical signs suggest secondary dysmenorrhoea? — Persistent pain despite NSAIDs, irregular bleeding, palpable pelvic mass, infertility.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a patient with dysmenorrhoea? — Fever >38 °C or sudden heavy bleeding with haemodynamic instability.
Explain why anovulatory cycles are usually painless. — Lack of ovulation means no luteal phase and minimal prostaglandin release.
How does a levonorgestrel‑releasing IUS improve dysmenorrhoea? — Provides local progestin, thinning endometrium and reducing prostaglandin production.
ai.title: Dysmenorrhoea
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Painful menstrual cramps caused by excess prostaglandins, most often primary but may signal secondary pathology. Assessment focuses on severity, red flags, and treatable causes, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Primary: no pelvic pathology, usually starts soon after menarche
Secondary: endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, congenital anomalies
sections.p: Dysmenorrhoea is recurrent crampy lower‑abdominal pain that starts with or shortly before menses and may radiate to the back or thighs. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history and exclusion of secondary causes.

b: Mild: VAS ≤3/10, does not interfere with daily activities
Moderate: VAS 4‑6/10, requires analgesia, some activity limitation
Severe: VAS ≥7/10, missed work/school, needs stronger therapy
sections.p: Severity is graded using a visual analogue scale (VAS) or a simple three‑point system to guide treatment.

b: Primary dysmenorrhoea – excess uterine prostaglandin F2α after ovulation
Endometriosis – ectopic endometrium, common in women with infertility
Adenomyosis – uterine wall infiltration, more in multiparous women
Uterine fibroids – especially submucosal, cause heavy flow and pain
Pelvic inflammatory disease – TB or bacterial infection, consider HIV co‑infection
Schistosomiasis of the genital tract – endemic in some East African regions
sections.p: Causes are grouped by primary versus secondary and by prevalence in low‑resource settings.

b: Crampy lower‑abdominal pain, often bilateral

sections.p: Pain begins 0‑2 days before menses, peaks in the first 24 hours, and may be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, headache, or low‑grade fever.
Investigations are directed at ruling out secondary causes; many can be done without sophisticated labs.

b: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) – inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, first‑line for primary pain
Combined oral contraceptive pill – suppress ovulation, reduce prostaglandin surge; avoid in active thrombo‑embolic disease
